newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU ministers reject beef package compromise.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers reject beef package compromise.

text.p: European Union farm ministers on Tuesday unanimously rejected a compromise to break a deadlock over measures to cut output and compensate beef farmers battered by the mad cow crisis, EU officials said.
The Irish EU presidency was preparing a fresh compromise to present later this evening.
"Our intention is to keep trying to get an agreement," an Irish official said, adding talks could go through the night.
But prospects of success looked remote.
The crisis was triggered by a British government announcement that the fatal cattle brain disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), could be transmitted to people.

"It's very difficult to see how we can get an agreement," said Gerard Kiely, European Commission agriculture spokesman. "Ministers are trying to spend money which doesn't exist. They are not dealing with the central problem of reducing output."
Ireland had suggested postponing cuts in aid to cereals farmers to help fund the beef package as well as easing a politically unpalatable reduction in production.
But member states complained the aid was too vague and disagreed over how production should be cut following a 15 percent drop in beef demand since the crisis broke in March.
British scientists last week provided more evidence that BSE was linked to a new variant of the human brain disorder, Creutzfeld-Jakob Disease.
"The draft compromise is unacceptable. It's even provocative," said French Farm Minister Philippe Vasseur.

Vasseur, under intense pressure from livestock farmers in central France, said Paris would reject any compromise that did not compensate beef producers for income losses due to the consumer scare over BSE.
But Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said he could live with the Irish compromise because it met the twin objectives of reducing output while respecting budgets.
"Politically unpalatable decisions are necessary," Fischler was quoted as telling ministers.
The EU's executive believes that payments to cereals farmers, notably for setting aside farmland, must be cut to finance the 1.3 billion Ecus ($1.6 billion) cost of the beef package in 1998.

But Germany, backed by all member states except Britain and Sweden, believes the aid cuts are unnecessary because savings can be made and advance payments to oilseed farmers in 1997 could be delayed to the next year.
In 1996 there was a farm underspend of 1.7 billion Ecus.
An Irish proposal to cut the limit on the amount of unwanted beef bought by the EU into public stores to 550,000 tonnes, from 720,000 tonnes would also bring savings.
Most member states rejected key measures to cut output, notably the so-called "Herod premium" for slaughtering new born calves, saying it would anger animal rights groups and stir public outrage.
But ministers were divided over weight limits and other details of alternative German proposals to promote early marketing of cattle.
